claim: Drosophila larvae display defecation cycles of stereotypic frequency.
source: Drosophila larvae display defecation cycles of stereotypic frequency, involving sequential contraction of hindgut and anal sphincter.
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral observations and measurements presented in the manuscript, including video recordings and quantitative analysis of defecation intervals.

claim: Defecation behavior involves sequential contraction of hindgut and anal sphincter.
source: Drosophila larvae display defecation cycles of stereotypic frequency, involving sequential contraction of hindgut and anal sphincter.
evidence: This is demonstrated through direct observation and imaging shown in Figure 1B,D and Video 1.

claim: The defecation behavior requires two groups of motor neurons that innervate hindgut and anal sphincter, respectively.
source: The defecation behavior requires two groups of motor neurons that innervate hindgut and anal sphincter, respectively, and can excite gut muscles directly.
evidence: This is supported by anatomical characterization, functional silencing experiments, and optogenetic activation experiments.

claim: PDF and HGN1 motor neurons can excite gut muscles directly.
source: The defecation behavior requires two groups of motor neurons that innervate hindgut and anal sphincter, respectively, and can excite gut muscles directly.
evidence: This is demonstrated by electrophysiological recordings showing excitatory junction potentials (EJPs) in gut muscles upon optogenetic activation of these neurons.

claim: PDF and HGN1 motor neurons fire sequentially with the same periodicity as the defecation behavior.
source: These two groups of motor neurons fire sequentially with the same periodicity as the defecation behavior, as revealed by in vivo Ca2+ imaging.
evidence: This is demonstrated by calcium imaging experiments showing rhythmic activity in both neuronal groups with 38-second intervals.

claim: A single mechanosensitive sensory neuron innervates the anal slit and senses the opening of the intestine terminus.
source: Moreover, we identified a single mechanosensitive sensory neuron that innervates the anal slit and senses the opening of the intestine terminus.
evidence: This is supported by anatomical characterization, calcium imaging showing responses to anus opening, and functional experiments.

claim: The anus sensory neuron relies on the TRP channel NOMPC for mechanotransduction.
source: This anus sensory neuron relies on the TRP channel NOMPC but not on INACTIVE, NANCHUNG, or PIEZO for mechanotransduction.
evidence: This is demonstrated by loss of calcium responses in nompC mutants and rescue by NOMPC expression.

claim: The anus sensory neuron does not rely on INACTIVE for mechanotransduction.
source: This anus sensory neuron relies on the TRP channel NOMPC but not on INACTIVE, NANCHUNG, or PIEZO for mechanotransduction.
evidence: This is demonstrated by normal calcium responses in iav mutants.

claim: The anus sensory neuron does not rely on NANCHUNG for mechanotransduction.
source: This anus sensory neuron relies on the TRP channel NOMPC but not on INACTIVE, NANCHUNG, or PIEZO for mechanotransduction.
evidence: This is demonstrated by normal defecation intervals in nan mutants.

claim: The anus sensory neuron does not rely on PIEZO for mechanotransduction.
source: This anus sensory neuron relies on the TRP channel NOMPC but not on INACTIVE, NANCHUNG, or PIEZO for mechanotransduction.
evidence: This is demonstrated by normal defecation intervals in piezo mutants.

claim: Defecation allows the body to eliminate waste, an essential step in food processing for animal survival.
source: Defecation allows the body to eliminate waste, an essential step in food processing for animal survival.
evidence: This is a general biological principle stated in the introduction.

claim: Defecation eliminates waste (feces) from the digestive tract via the anus.
source: It eliminates waste (feces) from the digestive tract via the anus (Thomas, 1990; Heaton et al., 1992; Lembo and Camilleri, 2003), an unglamorous but essential body function.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Malfunction of defecation can lead to constipation and other diseases.
source: Malfunction of defecation can lead to constipation and other diseases (Lembo and Camilleri, 2003), and abnormal development of neural circuits governing defecation may underlie birth defects such as Hirschsprung's disease due to elimination of intestinal ganglion cells required for bowel peristalsis (Romeo et al., 1994; Passarge, 2002), one of the major birth defects of the digestive system afflicting one in 4000 of the population.
evidence: This is supported by citations to medical literature.

claim: Hirschsprung's disease is due to elimination of intestinal ganglion cells required for bowel peristalsis.
source: Malfunction of defecation can lead to constipation and other diseases (Lembo and Camilleri, 2003), and abnormal development of neural circuits governing defecation may underlie birth defects such as Hirschsprung's disease due to elimination of intestinal ganglion cells required for bowel peristalsis (Romeo et al., 1994; Passarge, 2002), one of the major birth defects of the digestive system afflicting one in 4000 of the population.
evidence: This is supported by citations to medical literature.

claim: Hirschsprung's disease afflicts one in 4000 of the population.
source: Malfunction of defecation can lead to constipation and other diseases (Lembo and Camilleri, 2003), and abnormal development of neural circuits governing defecation may underlie birth defects such as Hirschsprung's disease due to elimination of intestinal ganglion cells required for bowel peristalsis (Romeo et al., 1994; Passarge, 2002), one of the major birth defects of the digestive system afflicting one in 4000 of the population.
evidence: This is supported by citations to medical literature.

claim: Drosophila larvae provide a useful model system for the studies of feeding behavior and nutrition intake.
source: Drosophila larvae provide a useful model system for the studies of feeding behavior and nutrition intake (Ikeya et al., 2002; Rulifson et al., 2002; Hwangbo et al., 2004; Bader et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: In Caenorhabditis elegans two groups of excitatory GABAergic motor neurons have been identified with partially redundant functions in activating enteric muscle cells (EMCs).
source: In Caenorhabditis elegans two groups of excitatory GABAergic motor neurons have been identified with partially redundant functions in activating enteric muscle cells (EMCs) (McIntire et al., 1993).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work in C. elegans.

claim: The Drosophila larval hindgut is the last part of the intestine, posterior to the Malpighian tubule, on the dorsal side under larval cuticle.
source: The Drosophila larval hindgut is the last part of the intestine, posterior to the Malpighian tubule, on the dorsal side under larval cuticle.
evidence: This is an anatomical description supported by the figures.

claim: The anal sphincter has a layer of thick sphincter muscles and a much narrower canal.
source: At the posterior end of the hindgut is anal sphincter, which has a layer of thick sphincter muscles and a much narrower canal (Figure 1A, Figure1—figure supplement 1) (Murakami and Shiotsuki, 2001).
evidence: This is supported by anatomical observations and citation to previous literature.

claim: The defecation process is repeated every 38 s at 25°C.
source: This defecation process is repeated every 38 s at 25°C (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by quantitative measurements shown in Figure 1D.

claim: PDF neurons and HGN1 neurons have their cell bodies in the terminal segments of VNC.
source: These neurons have their cell bodies in the terminal segments of VNC (Figure 1E) and send their axons along the midline of the ventral body wall to the posterior end of the larva, where they enter the hindgut.
evidence: This is demonstrated by anatomical imaging shown in Figure 1E.

claim: HGN1 axons extend posteriorly to the anus sphincter surface to form dense arborizations over the muscles.
source: Within the hindgut, the HGN1 axons extend posteriorly to the anus sphincter surface to form dense arborizations over the muscles, while the PDF axons arborize over the posterior two-third of the hindgut with refined branches (Figure 1F–H).
evidence: This is demonstrated by anatomical imaging shown in Figure 1F-H.

claim: PDF axons arborize over the posterior two-third of the hindgut with refined branches.
source: Within the hindgut, the HGN1 axons extend posteriorly to the anus sphincter surface to form dense arborizations over the muscles, while the PDF axons arborize over the posterior two-third of the hindgut with refined branches (Figure 1F–H).
evidence: This is demonstrated by anatomical imaging shown in Figure 1F-H.

claim: PDF and HGN1 neurons are glutamatergic.
source: The PDF and HGN1 neurons are glutamatergic, as they could be labeled with antibody staining against Drosophila vGlut (Daniels et al., 2008) (Figure 1K,L).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunostaining experiments shown in Figure 1K,L.

claim: Illumination of the larval VNC with blue light caused a dramatic increase of EJPs in the anus sphincter muscles in the larva with ChR2 expression in the HGN1 neurons.
source: Illumination of the larval VNC with blue light caused a dramatic increase of EJPs in the anus sphincter muscles in the larva with ChR2 expression in the HGN1 neurons but not in the control animals (Figure 2B,C), providing evidence for HGN1 innervation of sphincter muscles.
evidence: This is demonstrated by electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 2B,C.

claim: Activation of PDF neurons expressing ChR2 with blue light triggered a dramatic increase of EJPs in the anus sphincter muscles.
source: Activation of PDF neurons expressing ChR2 with blue light also triggered a dramatic increase of EJPs in the anus sphincter muscles (Figure 2B,C), indicating that PDF neurons also play a role in regulating anal sphincter contractions, although PDF neurons do not directly form synapse with these muscles.
evidence: This is demonstrated by electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 2B,C.

claim: PDF neurons do not directly form synapse with anal sphincter muscles.
source: Activation of PDF neurons expressing ChR2 with blue light also triggered a dramatic increase of EJPs in the anus sphincter muscles (Figure 2B,C), indicating that PDF neurons also play a role in regulating anal sphincter contractions, although PDF neurons do not directly form synapse with these muscles.
evidence: This is inferred from the anatomical observations showing PDF axons do not directly innervate the anal sphincter.

claim: Silencing PDF neurons caused the interval of the defecation to increase from 38 s to 94 s.
source: Silencing PDF neurons caused the interval of the defecation to increase from 38 s to 94 s (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by behavioral experiments using Kir2.1 to silence neurons, shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Silencing the HGN1 neurons did not significantly alter the interval of anus sphincter opening.
source: Silencing the HGN1 neurons did not significantly alter the interval of anus sphincter opening (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by behavioral experiments shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Silencing both the PDF neurons and HGN1 neurons caused the larva to display barely any hindgut movement over 5 min.
source: Indeed, silencing both the PDF neurons and HGN1 neurons caused the larva to display barely any hindgut movement over 5 min thus rendering it difficult to estimate the defecation interval, in contrast to the nearly eight cycles of contraction over 5 min—corresponding to a defecation interval of 38 s—in control animals (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by behavioral experiments shown in Figure 3B.

claim: PDF neurons displayed a stereotypical periodic firing pattern with an average interval between peak Ca2+ signals of 38 s.
source: Indeed, the PDF neurons displayed a stereotypical periodic firing pattern as revealed by Ca2+ elevation in both soma and dendrite area (Figure 4A,C). The average interval between peak Ca2+ signals is 38 s, which is highly consistent with the temporal pattern of contraction of the hindgut (Figure 1D and Figure 4M).
evidence: This is demonstrated by calcium imaging experiments shown in Figure 4A,C,M.

claim: HGN1 neurons exhibited oscillation of Ca2+ levels with a periodicity of 38 s.
source: We also monitored the Ca2+ signals of the HGN1 neurons and found that the HGN1 neurons also exhibited oscillation of Ca2+ levels with a periodicity of 38 s (Figure 4B,D,M, Video 3).
evidence: This is demonstrated by calcium imaging experiments shown in Figure 4B,D,M.

claim: Ca2+ signals of HGN1 neurons spread from dendrites to soma with a fixed latency.
source: Furthermore, Ca2+ signals of HGN1 neurons spread from dendrites to soma with a fixed latency (Video 3), indicating that the HGN1 neurons may receive excitatory inputs with a periodicity of 38 s.
evidence: This is demonstrated by calcium imaging shown in Video 3.

claim: HGN1 neurons may receive excitatory inputs with a periodicity of 38 s.
source: Furthermore, Ca2+ signals of HGN1 neurons spread from dendrites to soma with a fixed latency (Video 3), indicating that the HGN1 neurons may receive excitatory inputs with a periodicity of 38 s.
evidence: This is inferred from the pattern of calcium signal propagation.

claim: The arborizations of PDF neurons and HGN1 neurons overlap extensively along the midline of the posterior VNC.
source: The arborizations of PDF neurons and HGN1 neurons overlap extensively along the midline of the posterior VNC (Figure 4E,F and Video 4), raising the question whether they interact with each other.
evidence: This is demonstrated by anatomical imaging shown in Figure 4E,F and Video 4.

claim: An intense GFP signal was observed in the area where the processes of PDF and HGN1 neurons overlap using GRASP.
source: We expressed the two GFP components separately in PDF neurons and HGN1 neurons by using two different binary expression systems, PDF-LexA and HGN1-Gal4. An intense GFP signal was observed in the area where the processes of these two groups of neurons overlap (Figure 4G), while neither PDF neuron nor HGN1 neuron expressing one part of the split GFP of GRASP generated any fluorescent signals by itself (Figure 4—figure supplement 2), suggesting that a functional connection might exist between PDF and HGN1 neurons.
evidence: This is demonstrated by GRASP experiments shown in Figure 4G.

claim: A functional connection might exist between PDF and HGN1 neurons.
source: We expressed the two GFP components separately in PDF neurons and HGN1 neurons by using two different binary expression systems, PDF-LexA and HGN1-Gal4. An intense GFP signal was observed in the area where the processes of these two groups of neurons overlap (Figure 4G), while neither PDF neuron nor HGN1 neuron expressing one part of the split GFP of GRASP generated any fluorescent signals by itself (Figure 4—figure supplement 2), suggesting that a functional connection might exist between PDF and HGN1 neurons.
evidence: This is inferred from GRASP results indicating close proximity of neuronal processes.

claim: PDF neurons send their axons to the area where their processes overlap with HGN1 neuron dendrites.
source: By labeling the PDF neurons simultaneously with the dendritic RFP marker DenMark and the axonal GFP marker sytGFP, we found that the PDF neurons send their axons to the area where their processes overlap with HGN1 neuron dendrites (Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is demonstrated by dual labeling experiments shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: The Ca2+ level began to rise in PDF neuron cell bodies and then spread to the area occupied by arborizations of both groups of neurons, followed by Ca2+ elevation in the cell bodies of HGN1 neurons with a very short delay.
source: By monitoring the Ca2+ signals in PDF neurons and HGN1 neurons simultaneously, we found that the Ca2+ level began to rise in PDF neuron cell bodies and then spread to the area occupied by arborizations of both groups of neurons, followed by Ca2+ elevation in the cell bodies of HGN1 neurons with a very short delay, indicating that these two groups of neurons have coordinated firing patterns (Figure 4H–L and Video 5).
evidence: This is demonstrated by simultaneous calcium imaging shown in Figure 4H-L and Video 5.

claim: PDF neurons and HGN1 neurons have coordinated firing patterns.
source: By monitoring the Ca2+ signals in PDF neurons and HGN1 neurons simultaneously, we found that the Ca2+ level began to rise in PDF neuron cell bodies and then spread to the area occupied by arborizations of both groups of neurons, followed by Ca2+ elevation in the cell bodies of HGN1 neurons with a very short delay, indicating that these two groups of neurons have coordinated firing patterns (Figure 4H–L and Video 5).
evidence: This is inferred from the sequential calcium signals observed in the two neuronal groups.

claim: A specialized PPK-Gal4-labeled neuron was found in the vicinity of the anal slit.
source: In the vicinity of the anal slit, we found a specialized PPK-Gal4-labeled neuron.
evidence: This is demonstrated by anatomical characterization using PPK-Gal4 driver.

claim: The cell body of the anus sensory neuron resides on the anterior side of the anal slit, and its dendritic arbors surround the entire anal slit.
source: The cell body of this neuron resides on the anterior side of the anal slit, and its dendritic arbors surround the entire anal slit (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by anatomical imaging shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The majority of ASN dendrites forms a thin layer of arbors and covers the body wall around the anal slit.
source: The majority of its dendrites forms a thin layer of arbors and covers the body wall around the anal slit (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by anatomical imaging shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Some ASN arborizations extend along the anus sphincter.
source: There are also some arborizations extending along the anus sphincter (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by anatomical imaging shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The axon of the anus sensory neuron joins the nerve bundle that includes the axons of other da neurons and projects to the terminal segment of the VNC.
source: The axon of this sensory neuron joins the nerve bundle that includes the axons of other da neurons and projects to the terminal segment of the VNC.
evidence: This is demonstrated by anatomical tracing.

claim: When the anal slit opens, the ASN dendrites are dramatically stretched.
source: When the anal slit opens, the dendrites are dramatically stretched (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by imaging shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Opening of the anal slit is accompanied with Ca2+ elevation in both dendrites and soma of the ASN.
source: We found that opening of the anal slit is accompanied with Ca2+ elevation in both dendrites and soma of this neuron (Figure 5C,D and Video 6).
evidence: This is demonstrated by calcium imaging shown in Figure 5C,D and Video 6.

claim: The periodicity of ASN Ca2+ response is similar to that of the movements of the anus and the oscillations of PDF neurons and HGN1 neurons in the VNC.
source: The periodicity of this Ca2+ response is similar to that of the movements of the anus and the oscillations of PDF neurons and HGN1 neurons in the VNC (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by quantitative comparison shown in Figure 5E.

claim: The ASN is mechanosensitive and participates in sensing the radial stretch caused by opening the anus.
source: This result indicates that the ASN is mechanosensitive and participates in sensing the radial stretch caused by opening the anus.
evidence: This is inferred from the calcium responses observed when the anus opens.

claim: The ASN projects to the terminal segments of the VNC and its axon terminals overlap with the area occupied by the dendrites of the HGN1 neurons and PDF neurons.
source: This sensory neuron projects to the terminal segments of the VNC and its axon terminals overlap with the area occupied by the dendrites of the HGN1 neurons and PDF neurons (Figure 5F).
evidence: This is demonstrated by anatomical imaging shown in Figure 5F.

claim: There is very strong GRASP signal at the site where ASN axons and PDF dendrites overlap.
source: We found that there is very strong GRASP signal at the site where ASN axons and PDF dendrites overlap (Figure 5G), while neither PDF neurons nor ASN expressing one part of the split GFP of GRASP generated any fluorescent signals (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by GRASP experiments shown in Figure 5G.

claim: The GRASP signal between ASN and PDF neurons is asymmetric, in concordance with the localization of the ASN cell body to one side of the midline.
source: Interestingly, the GRASP signal is asymmetric, in concordance with the localization of the ASN cell body to one side of the midline leading to a more intense axonal projection to the ipsilateral VNC, which is also evident with asymmetric Ca2+ elevation of the ASN axon terminals in the VNC (Video 7).
evidence: This is demonstrated by GRASP imaging and calcium imaging shown in Video 7.

claim: Activation of ASN via blue light illumination induced large increases of EJPs in the majority of the anus sphincter muscles.
source: Activation of ASN via blue light illumination induced large increases of EJPs in the majority of the anus sphincter muscles (Figure 5H,I).
evidence: This is demonstrated by optogenetic activation and electrophysiological recording shown in Figure 5H,I.

claim: Both PDF and HGN1 neurons responded to mechanical stimulation of the anus with a glass probe.
source: We found that both PDF and HGN1 neurons responded to this local stimulation (Figure 5J).
evidence: This is demonstrated by calcium imaging during mechanical stimulation shown in Figure 5J.

claim: Laser ablation of ASN at 48 hr AEL completely abolished the ASN 48 hr after ablation, while the other PPK neurons remained intact.
source: The ASN was completely abolished 48 hr after laser ablation, while the other PPK neurons remained intact (Figure 5K).
evidence: This is demonstrated by imaging after laser ablation shown in Figure 5K.

claim: After ASN ablation, HGN1 neurons displayed abnormality of their rhythmic firing pattern with a much longer interval compared to control animals.
source: We then imaged the cell bodies of HGN1 neurons in the VNC and found abnormality of their rhythmic firing pattern, which displayed a much longer interval compared to control animals (Figure 5L).
evidence: This is demonstrated by calcium imaging after ASN ablation shown in Figure 5L.

claim: The sensory neuron in the anus might sense the stretch when the anal slit is open and respond by providing feedback modulation of the PDF neurons and HGN1 neurons in the central nervous system.
source: These results suggest that the central neurons in the VNC receive excitatory feedback from ASN to increase motor neuron firing. Together with the GRASP analysis revealing the physical proximity of the processes of ASN and PDF neurons, our results indicate that the sensory neuron in the anus might sense the stretch when the anal slit is open and respond by provide feedback modulation of the PDF neurons and HGN1 neurons in the central nervous system.
evidence: This is inferred from the combination of anatomical, functional, and ablation experiments.

claim: The defecation rhythm remains normal in the iav, nan, and piezo mutants.
source: We found that the defecation rhythm remains normal in the iav, nan, and piezo mutants.
evidence: This is demonstrated by behavioral measurements in mutant animals.

claim: The defecation interval in the nompC mutants was significantly increased.
source: However, the defecation interval in the nompC mutants was significantly increased (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by behavioral measurements shown in Figure 6A.

claim: NOMPC is a TRPN channel essential for adult hearing and larval gentle touch.
source: NOMPC is a TRPN channel essential for adult hearing and larval gentle touch (Gong et al., 2004; Yan et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: NOMPC is highly expressed all over the dendrites and soma of the ASN.
source: We found that NOMPC is highly expressed all over the dendrites and soma of the ASN, as revealed by staining with antibody against the NOMPC protein (Figure 6—figure supplement 1), raising the possibility that it might play a role in ASN sensing of radial stretch.
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunostaining shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: The Ca2+ response is absent in the ASN of nompC null mutant larvae.
source: Indeed, we found that the Ca2+ response is absent in the ASN of nompC null mutant larvae (Figure 6B,C, Video 8).
evidence: This is demonstrated by calcium imaging in nompC mutants shown in Figure 6B,C and Video 8.

claim: The defect in ASN Ca2+ response in nompC mutants could be rescued by expressing wild-type NOMPC in the ASN with PPK-Gal4.
source: This defect could be rescued by expressing wild-type NOMPC in the ASN with PPK-Gal4 (Figure 6B,C, Video 9).
evidence: This is demonstrated by rescue experiments shown in Figure 6B,C and Video 9.

claim: The ASN of iav1 mutant larvae exhibited Ca2+ response comparable to that in the wild-type larvae.
source: We found the ASN of iav1 mutant larvae exhibited Ca2+ response comparable to that in the wild-type larvae (Figure 6C and Video 10), suggesting that IAV is not required for the mechanotransduction of ASN.
evidence: This is demonstrated by calcium imaging in iav mutants shown in Figure 6C and Video 10.

claim: IAV is not required for the mechanotransduction of ASN.
source: We found the ASN of iav1 mutant larvae exhibited Ca2+ response comparable to that in the wild-type larvae (Figure 6C and Video 10), suggesting that IAV is not required for the mechanotransduction of ASN.
evidence: This is inferred from the normal calcium responses in iav mutants.

claim: Drosophila larvae exhibit rhythmic cycles of sequential contractions of the hindgut and the anal sphincter.
source: We found that Drosophila larvae exhibit periodic defecation cycles, involving sequential contractions of the hindgut and the anal sphincter.
evidence: This is a summary statement supported by the behavioral observations throughout the study.

claim: Two groups of neurons innervate the hindgut and anal sphincter respectively, and can excite the hindgut and anal sphincter muscle in a sequential manner.
source: We also found two groups of neurons, which innervate the hindgut and anal sphincter respectively, and can excite the hindgut and anal sphincter muscle in a sequential manner.
evidence: This is a summary statement supported by the anatomical and functional characterization throughout the study.

claim: A single sensory neuron could sense the opening of the anal slit and send feedback to the motor neurons.
source: In addition, we found a single sensory neuron that could sense the opening of the anal slit and send feedback to the motor neurons (Figure 7).
evidence: This is a summary statement supported by the characterization of the ASN throughout the study.

claim: At the larval stage, the motor neurons and gut muscles as well as the sensory neuron responding to anus movement, all show very robust rhythmic activities.
source: However, at the larval stage, the motor neurons and gut muscles as well as the sensory neuron responding to anus movement, all show very robust rhythmic activities.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on the calcium imaging and behavioral observations.

claim: Robust rhythmic feeding and defecation behaviors may facilitate larval nutrition intake and waste expulsion.
source: Given that feeding and defecation are dominant behaviors for third-instar larvae, conceivably robust rhythmic feeding and defecation behaviors may facilitate their nutrition intake and waste expulsion.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the observed robust rhythmic behaviors.

claim: Adult flies may need to conduct their defection behaviors in a more controllable manner due to encountering more complex environments.
source: In contrast, adult flies will likely encounter more complex environments and may need to conduct their defection behaviors in a more controllable manner.
evidence: This is a speculative comparison between larval and adult defecation behaviors.

claim: The ASN could be labeled by both class III da neuronal marker and class IV da neuronal maker.
source: Interestingly, the ASN could be labeled by both class III da neuronal marker and class IV da neuronal maker, raising the question whether it might have the dual functions to sense different stimuli.
evidence: This is stated as an observation that raises a question for future investigation.

claim: The two motor neurons appear to be functionally connected, possibly involving synaptic connections between them.
source: The two motor neurons appear to be functionally connected, possibly involving synaptic connections between them, although we cannot exclude the possibility of multiple neurons being engaged in their functional connections.
evidence: This is inferred from the GRASP results and sequential firing patterns, but acknowledged as uncertain.

claim: It remains to be determined as to how PDF and HGN1 neurons are entrained with this rhythmic firing pattern, and whether it involves a central pattern generator upstream of PDF neurons.
source: It remains to be determined as to how they are entrained with this rhythmic firing pattern, and whether it involves a central pattern generator upstream of PDF neurons.
evidence: This is stated as an open question for future research.

claim: PDF is a peptide that has important roles in multiple neuropeptide signaling pathways in the fruit fly.
source: Interestingly, PDF is a peptide that has important roles in multiple neuropeptide signaling pathways in the fruit fly (Renn et al., 1999; Kim et al., 2013); it would be interesting to test whether this neuropeptide also plays a role in the regulation of defecation behaviors by PDF neurons in the VNC.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: A recent study has suggested a novel role of HGN1 neurons in regulating the long-term food intake behaviors of adult flies.
source: Recently, a study has suggested a novel role of HGN1 neurons in regulating the long-term food intake behaviors of adult flies (Olds and Xu, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a recent study.

claim: HGN1 neurons control the rhythmic pattern of larval defecation.
source: In our study we found that HGN1 neurons control the rhythmic pattern of larval defecation.
evidence: This is a summary of findings from the current study.

claim: Drosophila HGN1 neurons at different developmental stages might have multiple functions in regulating feeding and defecation behaviors.
source: These two studies suggest that Drosophila HGN1 neurons at different developmental stages might have multiple functions in regulating feeding and defecation behaviors.
evidence: This is inferred from comparing the current study with previous work on HGN1 neurons.

claim: The structures of Drosophila gut and human gut share striking similarity.
source: Though separated in evolution millions years ago, the structures of Drosophila gut and human gut share striking similarity.
evidence: This is a general comparative statement based on anatomical knowledge.

claim: There are circular and longitudinal muscles lining the gut ending with the anal sphincter that controls defecation in both Drosophila and humans.
source: There are circular and longitudinal muscles lining the gut ending with the anal sphincter that controls defecation (Netter, 1997; Murakami and Shiotsuki, 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations to anatomical references.

claim: Diseases such as Hirschsprung's disease and anorectal malformation with failure to pass meconium are caused by developmental abnormality related to the gut and its innervation.
source: Diseases such as Hirschsprung's disease and anorectal malformation with failure to pass meconium (Loening-Baucke and Kimura, 1999) are caused by developmental abnormality related to the gut and its innervation.
evidence: This is supported by citation to medical literature.

claim: Mutations in two human genes could lead to the absence of certain nerve cells in the colon.
source: Mutations in two human genes could lead to the absence of certain nerve cells in the colon (Puri and Shinkai, 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citation to medical literature.

claim: The Drosophila larval body wall is transparent.
source: Because the Drosophila larval body wall is transparent, contractions of the hindgut and anal sphincter can be monitored in vivo.
evidence: This is a known property of Drosophila larvae that enables the experimental approach.

claim: Contractions of the hindgut and anal sphincter can be monitored in vivo in Drosophila larvae.
source: Because the Drosophila larval body wall is transparent, contractions of the hindgut and anal sphincter can be monitored in vivo.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the experimental approach used throughout the study.

claim: Each sequential contraction of hindgut and anus sphincter triggered a defecation cycle to expel feces out of the body.
source: As shown in Figure 1C and Video 1, each sequential contraction of hindgut and anus sphincter triggered a defecation cycle to expel feces out of the body.
evidence: This is demonstrated by video recordings shown in Figure 1C and Video 1.

claim: The axons that innervate the hindgut are from the most posterior pair of the axon bundles in the ventral nerve cord (VNC).
source: Since the axons that innervate the hindgut are from the most posterior pair of the axon bundles in the ventral nerve cord (VNC), the cell bodies of the neurons that innervate the hindgut and anal sphincter are most likely in the terminal segments of the VNC.
evidence: This is based on anatomical tracing observations.

claim: The cell bodies of the neurons that innervate the hindgut and anal sphincter are most likely in the terminal segments of the VNC.
source: Since the axons that innervate the hindgut are from the most posterior pair of the axon bundles in the ventral nerve cord (VNC), the cell bodies of the neurons that innervate the hindgut and anal sphincter are most likely in the terminal segments of the VNC.
evidence: This is inferred from the anatomical organization of the nervous system.

claim: PDF neurons and HGN1 neurons send their axons along the midline of the ventral body wall to the posterior end of the larva, where they enter the hindgut.
source: These neurons have their cell bodies in the terminal segments of VNC (Figure 1E) and send their axons along the midline of the ventral body wall to the posterior end of the larva, where they enter the hindgut.
evidence: This is demonstrated by anatomical tracing.

claim: The labeled neurons in both PDF and HGN1 cases have their axon terminals in close proximity of the gut muscles and form abundant bouton structures.
source: The labeled neurons in both cases have their axon terminals in close proximity of the gut muscles and form abundant bouton structures (Figure 1I,J).
evidence: This is demonstrated by high-resolution imaging shown in Figure 1I,J.

claim: PDF and HGN1 neurons are likely motor neurons that might play a role in regulating hindgut contractions.
source: These results suggest that PDF and HGN1 neurons, which are likely motor neurons, might play a role in regulating hindgut contractions (Figure 1M).
evidence: This is inferred from the anatomical and molecular characterization showing glutamatergic identity and innervation of gut muscles.

claim: The gut muscles received tonic excitatory inputs.
source: The gut muscles received tonic excitatory inputs (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The firing pattern of gut muscles might differ from those in intact animals due to the fillet recording methods used.
source: Due to the fillet recording methods we used to gain access of anus sphincter muscles, this firing pattern might differ from those in intact animals.
evidence: This is acknowledged as a potential limitation of the experimental approach.

claim: PDF neurons have been previously shown to promote visceral muscle contractions.
source: The PDF neurons have been previously shown to promote visceral muscle contractions (Talsma et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Light-induced activation of ChR2 in PDF or HGN1 neurons was absent in UAS or Gal4 control larvae and dependent on retinal.
source: This light-induced activation was absent in UAS or Gal4 control larvae and dependent on retinal, which is the chromosphere for ChR2 channels (Figure 2B,C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by control experiments shown in Figure 2B,C.

claim: Both the hindgut and anal sphincter contracted strongly upon blue light stimulation of PDF neurons expressing ChR2.
source: Both the hindgut and anal sphincter contracted strongly (Figure 2D) upon stimulation.
evidence: This is demonstrated by optogenetic experiments shown in Figure 2D.

claim: With ChR2 expression in the HGN1 neurons, the anal sphincter but not hindgut contracted upon blue light stimulation.
source: In contrast, with ChR2 expression in the HGN1 neurons, the anal sphincter but not hindgut contracted upon blue light stimulation of HGN1 neurons (Figure 2D and Video 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated by optogenetic experiments shown in Figure 2D and Video 2.

claim: The contractions induced by ChR2 activation were absent in larvae with only UAS-ChR2 or larvae fed with regular food without retinal.
source: The contractions were absent in larvae with only UAS-ChR2 or larvae fed with regular food without retinal.
evidence: This is demonstrated by control experiments.

claim: PDF neurons and HGN1 neurons are required for the normal defecation behavior.
source: These results suggest that the PDF neurons and HGN1 neurons are required for the normal defecation behavior.
evidence: This is inferred from the silencing experiments showing altered defecation patterns.

claim: Peristaltic hindgut movements driven by PDF neuronal activity could have generated sufficient pressure to force open the anus sphincter.
source: Conceivably the peristaltic hindgut movements driven by PDF neuronal activity could have generated sufficient pressure to force open the anus sphincter.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for why silencing HGN1 alone did not significantly affect defecation interval.

claim: HGN1 neurons displayed periodic Ca2+ activities in dissected VNC though with less regularity than in intact animals.
source: HGN1 neurons exhibited periodic Ca2+ activities though with less regularity in this isolated preparation (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by calcium imaging in dissected VNC shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: HGN1 neurons displayed clusters of EPSCs.
source: They also displayed clusters of EPSCs (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C), indicating that they received excitatory input from upstream neurons.
evidence: This is demonstrated by electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: HGN1 neurons received excitatory input from upstream neurons.
source: They also displayed clusters of EPSCs (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C), indicating that they received excitatory input from upstream neurons.
evidence: This is inferred from the presence of EPSCs in the recordings.

claim: HGN1 neurons fired bursts of action potentials.
source: Whole-cell patch recording of HGN1 neurons revealed that they fired bursts of action potentials (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D), similar to what was seen in other Drosophila larval motor neurons (Cattaert and Birman, 2001; Fox et al., 2006; Imlach et al., 2012).
evidence: This is demonstrated by electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1D.

claim: HGN1 neuronal firing pattern is similar to what was seen in other Drosophila larval motor neurons.
source: Whole-cell patch recording of HGN1 neurons revealed that they fired bursts of action potentials (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D), similar to what was seen in other Drosophila larval motor neurons (Cattaert and Birman, 2001; Fox et al., 2006; Imlach et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous electrophysiological studies.

claim: The cell bodies of PDF neurons are near the ventral surface of the VNC, while the cell bodies of HGN1 neurons are more dorsal and posterior.
source: The cell bodies of PDF neurons are near the ventral surface of the VNC, while the cell bodies of HGN1 neurons are more dorsal and posterior (Figure 4E), making it possible to distinguish the two groups of cell bodies when monitored laterally (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by anatomical imaging shown in Figure 4E.

claim: It is possible to distinguish PDF and HGN1 neuron cell bodies when monitored laterally.
source: The cell bodies of PDF neurons are near the ventral surface of the VNC, while the cell bodies of HGN1 neurons are more dorsal and posterior (Figure 4E), making it possible to distinguish the two groups of cell bodies when monitored laterally (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is inferred from the spatial separation of the two neuronal groups.

claim: The dendritic arborization (da) neurons are primary sensory neurons, which cover the entire body wall of a Drosophila larva.
source: The dendritic arborization (da) neurons are primary sensory neurons, which cover the entire body wall of a Drosophila larva.
evidence: This is established knowledge about da neurons in Drosophila larvae.

claim: Da neurons are important for sensing chemical, thermal, light, and mechanical stimulations.
source: They are important for sensing chemical, thermal, light, and mechanical stimulations (Tracey et al., 2003; Xiang et al., 2010; Kim et al., 2012; Yan et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Stimulation of the anus with a glass probe induced an asymmetric Ca2+ increase in the VNC that is consistent with the asymmetric projection of ASN axons.
source: Stimulation of the anus with this glass probe induced an asymmetric Ca2+ increase in the VNC that is consistent with the asymmetric projection of ASN axons (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated by calcium imaging during mechanical stimulation shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: The central neurons in the VNC receive excitatory feedback from ASN to increase motor neuron firing.
source: These results suggest that the central neurons in the VNC receive excitatory feedback from ASN to increase motor neuron firing.
evidence: This is inferred from the optogenetic activation and ablation experiments.

claim: NANCHUNG (NAN) and INACTIVE (IAV) are two TRP channels that often work in concert with NOMPC in other sensory neurons.
source: NANCHUNG (NAN) and INACTIVE (IAV), two other TRP channels that often work in concert with NOMPC in other sensory neurons, are thought to form heterodimers and function in the mechanotransduction in Drosophila (Gong et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: NAN and IAV are thought to form heterodimers and function in the mechanotransduction in Drosophila.
source: NANCHUNG (NAN) and INACTIVE (IAV), two other TRP channels that often work in concert with NOMPC in other sensory neurons, are thought to form heterodimers and function in the mechanotransduction in Drosophila (Gong et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: This study identified a new role of the NOMPC channel for sensing radial stretch of the intestinal terminus.
source: Our study thus identified a new role of the NOMPC channel, namely for sensing redial stretch of the intestinal terminus.
evidence: This is a summary of the novel finding regarding NOMPC function.

claim: Studies of C. elegans as a model system have investigated the defecation circuit.
source: Studies of C. elegans as a model system have investigated the defecation circuit (Thomas, 1990; Avery and Thomas, 1997; Branicky and Hekimi, 2006; Kwan et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous C. elegans studies.

claim: Studies of the adult fly have identified neurons regulating defecation behaviors subject to dietary and reproductive modulation.
source: Studies of the adult fly have identified neurons regulating defecation behaviors subject to dietary and reproductive modulation (Cognigni et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work on adult flies.

claim: The defecation rate of adult flies is regulated by both the internal state and environment, rather than showing a robust rhythm.
source: Previous studies of the defecation behaviors of the adult fly (Cognigni et al., 2011) have revealed that its defecation rate is regulated by both the internal state and environment, rather than showing a robust rhythm.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work on adult fly defecation.

claim: Feeding and defecation are dominant behaviors for third-instar larvae.
source: Given that feeding and defecation are dominant behaviors for third-instar larvae, conceivably robust rhythmic feeding and defecation behaviors may facilitate their nutrition intake and waste expulsion.
evidence: This is based on general knowledge of larval biology.

claim: Mechanosensation serves a number of important physiological functions in Drosophila larvae.
source: Mechanosensation serves a number of important physiological functions in Drosophila larvae.
evidence: This is general knowledge about sensory function.

claim: Radial stretch sensation is a special type of mechanosensation essential for the function of many organs with luminal structures such as the digestive system and the blood vessels.
source: The radial stretch sensation is a special type of mechanosensation essential for the function of many organs with luminal structures such as the digestive system and the blood vessels.
evidence: This is general physiological knowledge.

claim: How the organs sense radial stretch remains unclear.
source: However, how the organs sense radial stretch remains unclear.
evidence: This is stated as a gap in current knowledge that the study addresses.

claim: A sensory neuron that can sense radial stretch with highly specialized morphology has been identified in Drosophila larvae.
source: We have identified a sensory neuron that can sense radial stretch with its highly specialized morphology in Drosophila larvae.
evidence: This is a summary of the novel finding regarding the ASN.

claim: The ASN may provide a neuronal model to study the distinct and cooperative roles of different channels in a single neuron in the sensing of different intensity of stimulation.
source: The ASN may provide a neuronal model to study the distinct and cooperative roles of different channels in a single neuron in the sensing of different intensity of stimulation.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential future uses of the ASN as a model system.

claim: The two motor neurons and the sensory neuron ASN provide an entry point to elucidate defecation circuitry.
source: The two motor neurons and the sensory neuron ASN provide an entry point to elucidate defecation circuitry.
evidence: This is a summary statement about the significance of the findings.

claim: Multiple neurons may be engaged in the functional connections between PDF and HGN1 neurons.
source: The two motor neurons appear to be functionally connected, possibly involving synaptic connections between them, although we cannot exclude the possibility of multiple neurons being engaged in their functional connections.
evidence: This is acknowledged as an alternative possibility that cannot be excluded.

claim: It would be interesting to test whether PDF neuropeptide plays a role in the regulation of defecation behaviors by PDF neurons in the VNC.
source: Interestingly, PDF is a peptide that has important roles in multiple neuropeptide signaling pathways in the fruit fly (Renn et al., 1999; Kim et al., 2013); it would be interesting to test whether this neuropeptide also plays a role in the regulation of defecation behaviors by PDF neurons in the VNC.
evidence: This is stated as a question for future investigation.

claim: It is of interest to explore possible contributions of indirect effects of PDF over muscle contraction, such as an influence of tracheal branching in the hindgut that may affect muscle contractions.
source: It is also of interest to explore possible contributions of indirect effects of PDF over muscle contraction, such as an influence of tracheal branching in the hindgut that may affect muscle contractions (Linneweber et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated as a question for future investigation, with citation to relevant work.

claim: It remains an open question as to the extent of similarity of the mechanisms that control the gut movements between Drosophila and humans.
source: It remains an open question as to the extent of similarity of the mechanisms that control the gut movements.
evidence: This is stated as an open question for future research.

claim: Several genes and specific regions on the chromosomes have been shown or suggested to be associated with Hirschsprung's disease.
source: Several genes and specific regions on the chromosomes have been shown or suggested to be associated with Hirschsprung's disease.
evidence: This is general medical knowledge about genetic factors in Hirschsprung's disease.

claim: Further study of the Drosophila larval gut rhythmicity and its neural modulation will help identify evolutionarily conserved features as well as strategies that may have been adopted by different organisms for their fitness.
source: With the powerful genetic tools, further study of the Drosophila larval gut rhythmicity and its neural modulation will help us identify evolutionarily conserved features as well as strategies that may have been adopted by different organisms for their fitness.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the potential impact of future research.
